title: Carry and overflow are different
prompt: Add the four-bit patterns 1011 and 1101. Keep only four result bits. Give, in order: the carry out; signed two’s-complement overflow (1=yes, 0=no).
rules: Enter 2 comma-separated integers in the stated order. Spaces and leading zeroes are accepted. No units or formulas.
explanation: Unsigned 11+13=24=16+8, so the four-bit result is 1000 and the carry out is 1. As signed operands, −5+(−3)=−8, exactly the four-bit lower bound. Both inputs and the result are negative, so signed overflow is 0.

title: An address is not its contents
prompt: RBP=4096 and the qword at address 4080 contains 37. Execute leaq -16(%rbp), %rax, then movq -16(%rbp), %rbx. Give final RAX, then RBX, in decimal. No other writes occur.
rules: Enter 2 comma-separated integers in the stated order. Spaces and leading zeroes are accepted. No units or formulas.
explanation: RBP−16=4080. LEA computes that address without reading memory, so RAX=4080. MOV reads the qword stored at 4080, so RBX=37. RBP and memory stay unchanged.

title: Split an address into cache fields
prompt: A cache uses eight-bit byte addresses, eight-byte blocks, four sets and two ways. Split address 0xB6 into its tag, set index and byte offset. Give the three field VALUES as decimal integers, in that order.
rules: Enter 3 comma-separated integers in the stated order. Spaces and leading zeroes are accepted. No units or formulas.
explanation: 0xB6 is 182, or binary 10110110. Eight bytes per block need 3 offset bits; four sets need 2 index bits. Split as 101 | 10 | 110: tag 5, index 2, offset 6. The two ways share a set and add no address-index bit.

title: Test implication directions
prompt: At the single valuation p=false, q=true, evaluate in order: p→q; q→p; ¬q→¬p. Use 1 for true and 0 for false. This is a fixed evaluation; one agreeing row alone does not prove equivalence.
rules: Enter 3 comma-separated integers in the stated order. Spaces and leading zeroes are accepted. No units or formulas.
explanation: With p=false and q=true, p→q is true because its antecedent is false. q→p is false because it has a true antecedent and false consequent. ¬q→¬p is true. The converse differs; the contrapositive agrees on every valuation, not just this one.

title: Constant, assignment and quantifier
prompt: D={a,b} with a and b distinct; constant c denotes a; P is true exactly on {a}. A free variable x is assigned b. Evaluate in order: P(c); P(x) under that assignment; ∀x P(x). Use 1 for true and 0 for false.
rules: Enter 3 comma-separated integers in the stated order. Spaces and leading zeroes are accepted. No units or formulas.
explanation: The structure fixes c as a, and P(a) is true. The supplied assignment gives free x the object b, so P(x) is false. ∀x checks both objects independently of that free-variable assignment and fails at b. A named constant and a free variable are different roles.

title: Count objects at the right level
prompt: Let A={∅}. Give, in order: the number of elements of A; the number of elements of its powerset 𝒫(A); the number of ordered pairs in A×∅.
rules: Enter 3 comma-separated integers in the stated order. Spaces and leading zeroes are accepted. No units or formulas.
explanation: A contains one object: the empty set. Its subsets are ∅ and {∅}, so 𝒫(A) has 2 elements. A×∅ has no ordered pairs because a second coordinate cannot be chosen from the empty set.
